rationale: This row's loan status — overdue — is carried entirely by its background tint (.row-overdue), decoded by a colour key beneath the table. The words "overdue" appear nowhere in the row, and the table has only two columns (Title, Due), so a reader who cannot distinguish the tints has no way to learn that this item is overdue. The cells inside the row inherit the colour rather than owning it, so the row is the only element on the page where this can be judged.
The same row with a third column carrying a text badge that states the status in words. Colour still distinguishes the rows, but it is no longer the only thing that does — which is all 1.4.1 asks.

The "Name" field is marked required by rendering its label in red and nothing else. There is no asterisk, no "(required)" in the text, and no `required` or `aria-required` on the control — so the obligation is invisible to anyone who cannot see the colour difference, and invisible to assistive technology as well. The user learns the field was required when the form rejects it.
The same "Name" label says "required" in words and the control carries aria-required="true". The colour is now reinforcement rather than the sole carrier.

The Fenner Road series is told apart from the other two by stroke colour alone: no dash pattern, no direct label on the line, and the only key is a colour legend beside the chart. Two of the three colours are a red and a green of similar lightness. That is a coverage gap in the platform, not a model error, and it is the reason this record exists.

The rejected field is marked by a red border and nothing else — no aria-invalid, no aria-describedby, no error note in the DOM, no live region, and no change of text. A reader who cannot see the border colour cannot tell which of the fields the form objected to, and assistive technology is told nothing at all.
The same field with aria-invalid="true" and an aria-describedby resolving to a note that states the reason in words. The border colour is reinforcement.

The Renew column shows this item as a coloured ring meaning it cannot be renewed. There IS a second cue — the shapes differ, a ring against a filled dot — so colour is not strictly the only channel, which is the letter of 1.4.1. But neither shape is explained anywhere on the page and the indicator carries no text, so a reader who sees the difference still cannot decode it. Whether an unexplained second cue satisfies the criterion is genuinely arguable; a confident verdict either way over-claims.

rationale: This charge of GBP 4.20 is still owed, and the only thing on the page that says so is that the amount is printed in red. The line carries the date, the title and the reason; it does not carry the state. A key beneath the list explains that red means owed and green means settled, which helps only a reader who can already tell the two apart — a colour key is still colour. Measured as rendered: the two colours differ in hue and are all but identical in lightness, so they do not separate in greyscale either.
